title: Prepositions and the object marker

objectives.can: Read the common prepositions with and without suffixes, and recognise אֵת marking a definite object.
Recognise the commonest prepositions and particles.

explanation.summary: Prepositions say how a noun or pronoun relates to the rest of the clause: to, from, on, with, under, between. Hebrew nouns have no case endings, so the preposition alone carries the relation. A small word, אֵת, does a different job: it marks a definite direct object and has no English equivalent.

sections.heading: Prepositions before a noun
body: A preposition stands before the noun it governs, and the noun does not change its form. Some prepositions are separate words (אֶל, עַל, עַד, עִם); some are written on the front of the noun (בְּ, לְ, כְּ, and מִ- for 'from', which you met in the lesson on the article and the prefixed particles). A separate word is often joined to the next by a maqqef, as in אֶל־ and עַל־.

The sense of a preposition depends on its context and on the verb it follows. The glosses in the table below are the commonest senses, not complete definitions. For example, עַל means 'on' or 'over' in a plain description of place, but after some verbs it means 'against' or 'concerning'.

head: Preposition
Common senses
With a suffix
rows: until, as far as, up to

sections.heading: Prepositions with suffixes
body: A pronoun that follows a preposition is written as an ending on it, the same kind of ending you met on nouns. The result is one word: אֵלָיו is 'to him', עִמּוֹ is 'with him', לְךָ is 'to you' or 'for you'. The person, gender and number are read from the ending, and each preposition has its own stem before the suffix.

Most prepositions lengthen or change their stem before a suffix, so the form is sometimes hard to see. מִן becomes מִמֶּנִּי 'from me'; אֶל becomes אֵלָיו; אַחַר, in the form אַחֲרֵי, becomes אַחֲרָיו. Learn each as a pair, the plain form and the suffixed forms, rather than by a rule.

The prepositions ל and ב are written on the noun when they have one. They appear as separate words when a suffix is attached: לוֹ, לִי, לָהֶם, בּוֹ, בָּהֶם. In these forms you have to recognise the preposition from the vowel and the ending.

sections.heading: The object marker אֵת
body: In prose the word אֵת, usually written אֶת־ with a maqqef, stands before a direct object that is definite: a noun with the article, a proper name, a noun with a pronominal suffix, or a construct chain whose last member is definite. In Genesis 1:1 it stands before 'the heavens' and 'the earth'. It is not a preposition and is not translated into English; it tells you that the next word is the object of the verb, not its subject. It is less regular in poetry.

The object marker can take a suffix, and then it stands for an object pronoun: אֹתוֹ is 'him' and אֹתָם is 'them', as the object of a verb. In Genesis 1:27 God creates the man and 'him' (אֹתוֹ) is the object of the verb 'created'.

sections.heading: Two words that look alike
body: There is another אֵת, a preposition meaning 'with', and it is spelled the same: אֵת or אֶת־. Its suffixed forms are told apart by their vowels. The preposition has the stem אִתּ- (אִתּוֹ 'with him', אִתִּי 'with me'). The object marker has the stem אֹת- or אוֹת- (אֹתוֹ 'him', אֹתִי 'me').

Without a suffix the two cannot be told apart by their letters. The verb decides. A verb of walking, staying or speaking with someone points to 'with' (Genesis 5:22 and 6:9, 'walked with God'). A verb that takes a direct object points to the object marker. Genesis 5:22 shows both in one verse.

misunderstandings: אֶת־ does not mean 'with' when it marks an object, and it is never the English word 'the'. Look at the verb and at the noun that follows it.
A preposition with a suffix is one word, not two. אֵלָיו is not 'to' plus a separate 'him'; the ending is part of the word.
A Hebrew preposition has no single English equivalent. מִן is 'from' but also 'than'; עַל is 'on' but also 'against'. Read the verb and the noun with it.
The object marker is not a sign of any case. Hebrew nouns have no case endings, and אֵת does not give the noun one.

deeper.heading: Two prepositions in a row
body: Hebrew often joins two prepositions to make a more exact one. In Genesis 1:7 מִתַּחַת is 'from under' and מֵעַל is 'from upon'. The first part is מִן written on the front of the second preposition. The English translation often needs a single word for the whole.

deeper.heading: Repeating בֵּין
body: 'Between A and B' is said with בֵּין repeated before each member, as in 'between the light and between the darkness' in Genesis 1:4. A pronoun suffix follows the same pattern: בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ is 'between me and you'.

examples.analysis: אֵת stands before הַשָּׁמַיִם, 'the heavens', and again, as וְאֵת, before הָאָרֶץ, 'the earth'. Both nouns have the article and both are objects of the verb 'created'. The marker is not translated.

examples.analysis: The same spelling אֶת occurs twice in one verse with two different jobs. The first, before הָאֱלֹהִים, is the preposition 'with' ('walked with God'). The second, before מְתוּשֶׁלַח, marks the object of the verb 'begot'. The verb in each clause decides which it is.

examples.analysis: אֶת marks the object הָאָדָם at the start. At the end, אֹתוֹ and אֹתָם are the object marker with suffixes: 'him' and 'them', the objects of 'created'. The vowels אֹת- tell you this is the object marker and not the preposition 'with'.

examples.analysis: Four prepositional phrases in a short verse. עַד is 'until' (here before a verbal noun). אֶל is 'to', with הָאֲדָמָה. מִמֶּנָּה is מִן with a feminine singular suffix, 'from it', where 'it' is the ground. וְאֶל is 'and to', with the next noun עָפָר.

examples.analysis: אֵלָיו is אֶל with the 3rd masculine singular suffix: the LORD speaks 'to him'. לְךָ is ל with the 2nd masculine singular suffix, 'to you'. The word אֶת before הָאָרֶץ is the object marker, again before a noun with the article.

reading.why: The first ten verses use the object marker אֵת, עַל־ פְּנֵי, בֵּין repeated, מִתַּחַת, מֵעַל and אֶל in a text you may already know, so that each one can be found and named.

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: Now the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And God saw the light, that it was good; and God divided the light from the darkness.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, one day.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And God said: 'Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament; and it was so.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And God called the firmament Heaven. And there was evening and there was morning, a second day.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And God said: 'Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear.' And it was so.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And God called the dry land Earth, and the gathering together of the waters called He Seas; and God saw that it was good.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

authoring.by: Written for Ecclesia by Claude (Anthropic), following the public-domain grammars listed as sources. Every Hebrew word shown as an example, in a paradigm or in an exercise is taken from the Westminster Leningrad Codex as analysed by the Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible project.
